entries.term: defining relative clause: the woman who called
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A defining relative clause tells the listener which person or thing you mean: *the woman who called* is one particular woman, not any woman.
entries.usage: Use no commas, because the clause is part of the noun phrase; without it, the sentence is unclear or means something else. Use *who* or *that* for people and *that* or *which* for things (*that* is the usual American choice). German and Russian put a comma before every relative clause; English uses no comma before a defining one.
entries.pattern: noun + who / that / which + rest of the clause (no commas)
examples: **The woman who called this morning** wants to move her appointment to Friday.
Kids **who eat a good breakfast** usually concentrate better in class.
Is this **the charger that came with your phone**, or is it mine?

drill.sentence: {{The coffee shop that opened on our corner}} already has a line out the door every morning.
drill.hint: Join with that: A coffee shop opened on our corner. It already has a line out the door every morning.

mistake.wrong: The students, who failed the test, can take it again next week.
mistake.right: The students who failed the test can take it again next week.
mistake.why: With commas, the clause becomes extra information and suggests that all the students failed; a clause that says which ones takes no commas.

entries.term: non-defining relative clause: My sister, who lives in Ohio, …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A non-defining relative clause adds extra information about a person or thing that is already clear; the sentence still works without it.
entries.usage: Put commas around the clause (short pauses in speech) and use *who* for people and *which* for things; *that* is not possible here, and the pronoun can never be dropped. It is common in writing, news and careful speech; in casual conversation, people often use two separate sentences instead.
entries.pattern: noun, who / which + clause, … (commas; never that)
examples: My brother, **who lives in Denver**, is driving down for Thanksgiving.
Our old minivan, **which we bought in 2009**, finally died last week.
Dr. Patel, **who has been my doctor for twenty years**, is retiring in June.

drill.sentence: The museum's new wing, {{which cost forty million dollars}}, opens to the public next month.
drill.hint: Add the second sentence as extra information: The museum's new wing opens to the public next month. It cost forty million dollars.

mistake.wrong: Our CEO, that founded the company in 1998, is stepping down.
mistake.right: Our CEO, who founded the company in 1998, is stepping down.
mistake.why: Between commas, use *who* for people and *which* for things; *that* only introduces defining clauses.

entries.term: leaving out the object pronoun: the book I read
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: When the relative pronoun is the object of its clause, so that a new subject follows it, it can be left out: *the book (that) I read*.
entries.usage: Leaving it out is the normal choice in conversation and very common in writing; *the movie we saw* sounds more natural than *the movie which we saw*. It works only in defining clauses, never between commas. A preposition stays at the end of the clause: *the person I talked to*.
entries.pattern: noun + (that / who / which) + subject + verb (+ preposition)
examples: Is that **the jacket you bought** in Chicago last winter?
**The guy I sat next to** on the plane snored the whole flight.
Everybody loved **the soup you made** for the potluck.

drill.sentence: {{The restaurant we went to}} last night was way too loud.
drill.hint: Join without who, which or that: We went to a restaurant last night. It was way too loud.

mistake.wrong: The woman I talked yesterday is my new manager.
mistake.right: The woman I talked to yesterday is my new manager.
mistake.why: When the pronoun is dropped, the preposition still stays at the end of the clause.

entries.term: no extra pronoun in relative clauses: the book that I bought
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: The relative pronoun already stands for the noun, so the clause does not repeat it with *it, him, her* or *them*: *the book that I bought*, not *the book that I bought it*.
entries.usage: An extra pronoun sounds clearly foreign in planned speech. Natives sometimes produce one in long, tangled spoken sentences, but in writing it is always an error. Check long clauses carefully: the place after the verb where the object would normally go stays empty.
entries.pattern: noun + that / who / which + subject + verb (no it / him / them)
examples: I finally finished **the novel that you lent me**.
**The car that we rented** in Phoenix had a cracked windshield.
**The apartment that we looked at** yesterday had almost no closet space.

drill.sentence: The phone {{that I bought}} last month already has a cracked screen.
drill.hint: Correct the sentence: The phone that I bought it last month already has a cracked screen.

mistake.wrong: The guy who we bought our car from him was really nice.
mistake.right: The guy who we bought our car from was really nice.
mistake.why: *Who* already stands for the guy, so *him* repeats the object of *from*.

entries.term: where in relative clauses: the city where I grew up
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After a noun for a place, *where* introduces a relative clause and means *in which* or *at which*: *the city where I grew up*.
entries.usage: Normal in all registers; *in which* sounds formal, and *the city I grew up in* is the casual alternative. *Where* replaces the whole prepositional phrase, so nothing like *in* or *there* is added at the end. It also works with situations: *a point where*, *a case where*.
entries.pattern: place noun + where + subject + verb (= in / at which)
examples: This is the café **where we had our first date**.
I'd love to see the house **where my mom grew up**.
We need a yard **where the kids can run around** safely.

drill.sentence: That's the beach {{where we got engaged}}, so it's a special place for us.
drill.hint: Rewrite with where: That's the beach that we got engaged on, so it's a special place for us.

mistake.wrong: Boston is the city where I grew up in.
mistake.right: Boston is the city where I grew up.
mistake.why: *Where* already includes the preposition, so do not add *in* at the end (or say *the city I grew up in*).

entries.term: although / even though + clause: Although it was late, we kept going
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Although* introduces a fact that contrasts with the main clause, which is true anyway; *even though* means the same but stresses the surprise.
entries.usage: Both take a full clause with a subject and a verb and can come first (followed by a comma) or after the main clause. *Even though* is more emphatic and very common in speech, *although* sounds a little more formal, and *though* alone is the most casual.
entries.pattern: although / even though + subject + verb, main clause / main clause + although / even though + clause
examples: **Although she's only twelve**, she already reads at a college level.
He still went to work **even though he had a fever**.
**Even though we left at six**, we got stuck in traffic for an hour.

drill.sentence: We kept hiking {{even though}} it was getting dark.
drill.hint: Join with a two-word linker that stresses the surprise (not although): It was getting dark, but we kept hiking.

mistake.wrong: Although the rain, we went for a walk.
mistake.right: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
mistake.why: *Although* needs a full clause with a subject and a verb; before a noun alone, use *despite*.

entries.term: despite / in spite of + noun: Despite the rain, we went
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Despite* and *in spite of* introduce something that you would expect to stop the main action, but it doesn't; they are followed by a noun phrase.
entries.usage: *Despite* is the more common choice, especially in writing and news; *in spite of* means exactly the same. Neither can take a subject + verb directly (*despite it rained* is wrong), so use *although* for a clause. There is no *of* after *despite*.
entries.pattern: despite / in spite of + noun phrase, main clause
examples: **Despite the long wait**, the food was worth it.
The game went ahead **in spite of the snow**.
**Despite her injury**, she finished the marathon in under four hours.

drill.sentence: {{Despite the heavy traffic}}, we made it to the airport on time.
drill.hint: Rewrite with despite + noun: Although the traffic was heavy, we made it to the airport on time.

mistake.wrong: Despite of the cold, we ate outside on the porch.
mistake.right: Despite the cold, we ate outside on the porch.
mistake.why: *Despite of* mixes the two forms: say *despite* or *in spite of*.

entries.term: despite + -ing: Despite feeling sick, she came
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Despite* (or *in spite of*) + *-ing* contrasts something the subject does or is with the result: *Despite feeling sick, she came* means she felt sick but came anyway.
entries.usage: Common in writing and fairly formal speech; in conversation, *even though she felt sick* is more usual. The *-ing* form must have the same subject as the main clause. With an adjective, add *being* (*despite being tired*); for an earlier action, *having* + past participle also works (*despite having trained for months*).
entries.pattern: despite / in spite of + -ing (same subject as the main clause), main clause
examples: **Despite feeling nervous**, he gave a great speech at his sister's wedding.
She got the job **despite having no experience** in sales.
**In spite of living next door** for ten years, we've hardly ever talked.

drill.sentence: {{Despite being exhausted}}, I couldn't fall asleep last night.
drill.hint: Rewrite with despite + -ing: Although I was exhausted, I couldn't fall asleep last night.

mistake.wrong: Despite being late, the teacher let me into the exam.
mistake.right: Even though I was late, the teacher let me into the exam.
mistake.why: The *-ing* form refers to the subject of the main clause, so this sentence says the teacher was late.

entries.term: however as a connector: It's expensive. However, it works.
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *However* at the start of a sentence introduces a contrast with the previous sentence; it links sentences, not clauses inside one sentence.
entries.usage: More formal than *but*; common in emails, reports and essays, and less common in casual speech, where people say *but* or *though*. Put a period or semicolon before *however* and a comma after it. A comma alone before it (*…, however …*) is a comma splice, a punctuation error in edited writing.
entries.pattern: Sentence. However, sentence. / clause; however, clause
examples: The train takes longer. **However**, it's much cheaper than flying.
We'd love to help. **However**, we can't promise anything before March.
Most patients recovered within a week; **however**, a few needed a second round of treatment.

drill.sentence: The museum is usually free. {{However}}, special exhibitions cost fifteen dollars.
drill.hint: Split into two sentences with a formal contrast word: The museum is usually free, but special exhibitions cost fifteen dollars.

mistake.wrong: The hotel was nice, however the breakfast was terrible.
mistake.right: The hotel was nice. However, the breakfast was terrible.
mistake.why: *However* is not a conjunction like *but*; it needs a period or semicolon before it and a comma after it.

entries.term: to-infinitive of purpose: I came to see you
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *To* + base verb after a clause says why someone does something: *I came to see you* means I came because I wanted to see you.
entries.usage: The most common way to express purpose, in every register. Use *to* + verb, not *for* + verb or *for to* + verb; *for* goes before a noun (*I came for the party*). *In order to* is a more formal, more explicit version.
entries.pattern: main clause + to + base verb (purpose)
examples: I stopped by **to drop off** your mail.
She's working two jobs **to save up** for a car.
We called the hotel **to ask** about late check-in.

drill.sentence: I'm going to the pharmacy {{to pick up}} my prescription.
drill.hint: Join, saying why: I'm going to the pharmacy. I want to pick up my prescription.

mistake.wrong: I went to the store for buy milk.
mistake.right: I went to the store to buy milk.
mistake.why: Purpose with a verb is *to* + verb; *for* goes before a noun (*for milk*).

entries.term: in order to: We cut costs in order to survive
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *In order to* + base verb expresses purpose like *to*, but makes it explicit that the action is done to reach that goal.
entries.usage: Common in formal writing, instructions and official language; in conversation it can sound heavy, so people usually just say *to*. It is useful at the start of a sentence (*In order to apply, …*) and in the negative (*in order not to*). It cannot take its own subject; for a different subject, use *so that*.
entries.pattern: in order to + base verb
examples: **In order to qualify** for the discount, you need to show a student ID.
The city closed two lanes **in order to repair** the bridge.
We randomly assigned participants to groups **in order to reduce** bias.

drill.sentence: {{In order to}} renew your passport, you'll need a recent photo.
drill.hint: Make the purpose more formal and explicit: To renew your passport, you'll need a recent photo.

mistake.wrong: I spoke slowly in order to everyone understand me.
mistake.right: I spoke slowly so that everyone could understand me.
mistake.why: *In order to* cannot take its own subject; for a new subject, use *so that* + clause (or *in order for everyone to understand*).

entries.term: so that + can / could: I left early so that I could catch the train
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *So that* + subject + modal introduces a purpose clause: *I left early so that I could catch the train* means I left early because I wanted to catch it.
entries.usage: Use it when the purpose has its own subject or needs a modal (*so that the kids can sleep*). Use *can* or *will* after a present or future main verb, and *could* or *would* after a past one. In speech, *that* is often dropped (*so I could*), but there is no comma before it.
entries.pattern: main clause + so (that) + subject + can / could / will / would + verb
examples: I'll print an extra copy **so that you can** take one home.
We moved the couch **so that the dog couldn't** get behind it.
Speak into the microphone **so that everyone in the back can hear** you.

drill.sentence: I left the porch light on {{so that you could}} find the house in the dark.
drill.hint: Join with a purpose clause: I left the porch light on. I wanted you to be able to find the house in the dark.

mistake.wrong: I set two alarms so that I can wake up on time, but I still overslept.
mistake.right: I set two alarms so that I could wake up on time, but I still overslept.
mistake.why: The purpose belongs to the past, so use *could* (or *would*), not *can*.

entries.term: because vs. because of: because it rained / because of the rain
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Because* is followed by a clause with a subject and a verb; *because of* is followed by a noun or pronoun. Both introduce a reason.
entries.usage: Both are neutral and very common; *due to* is a more formal alternative to *because of*. In casual speech, *because* is often shortened to *'cause* (*cuz* in texts). Check what follows: *because the bus was late*, but *because of the late bus*.
entries.pattern: because + subject + verb / because of + noun or pronoun
examples: Our flight was delayed **because of a storm** in Atlanta.
I'm drinking decaf **because I couldn't sleep** last night.
She moved to Austin **because of her job**, but now she loves it there.

drill.sentence: Practice was canceled {{because of}} the heat.
drill.hint: Choose because or because of: Practice was canceled ___ the heat.

mistake.wrong: I couldn't sleep because the noise from the street.
mistake.right: I couldn't sleep because of the noise from the street.
mistake.why: *Because* alone needs a subject and a verb; before a noun, use *because of*.

entries.term: due to + noun: The delay was due to the weather
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Due to* + noun means *because of* and names the cause of something: *The delay was due to the weather*.
entries.usage: Typical of announcements, news and official messages (*due to circumstances beyond our control*); in conversation, *because of* is more common. Traditional usage guides allowed *due to* only after *be* (*The delay was due to …*); today *due to* meaning *because of* (*canceled due to rain*) is standard, though a few strict guides still object. Like *because of*, it takes a noun phrase, not a subject + verb.
entries.pattern: be due to + noun / due to + noun, main clause
examples: **Due to a signal problem**, the 8:15 train to Boston has been canceled.
Most of the damage **was due to water**, not fire.
The store is closed today **due to a power outage**.

drill.sentence: Most of this morning's flight delays {{were due to}} fog.
drill.hint: Rewrite with due to: Fog caused most of this morning's flight delays.

mistake.wrong: Due to the roads were icy, schools closed early.
mistake.right: Due to the icy roads, schools closed early.
mistake.why: *Due to* is followed by a noun phrase; with a subject and a verb, use *because* (*because the roads were icy*).

entries.term: so vs. such: so tired / such a long day
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Both make a quality stronger: *so* goes before an adjective or adverb alone (*so tired*), *such* before a noun phrase (*such a long day*, *such nice people*).
entries.usage: Very common in conversation to show emotion (*It was so good!*, *She's such a sweetheart*). With a singular countable noun, *a/an* comes after *such* (*such a mess*); with plural or uncountable nouns, there is no article (*such good weather*).
entries.pattern: so + adjective / adverb; such (a / an) + (adjective) + noun
examples: The kids were **so excited** about the first snow of the year.
We had **such a great time** at your party!
They're **such nice people**; I'm really glad they moved in next door.

drill.sentence: I almost fell asleep in the theater. It was {{such a boring movie}}!
drill.hint: Rewrite with such: I almost fell asleep in the theater. The movie was so boring!

mistake.wrong: It was a such beautiful day, so we went to the lake.
mistake.right: It was such a beautiful day, so we went to the lake.
mistake.why: *A/an* comes after *such*, not before it.

entries.term: too vs. not enough: too small / not big enough
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Too* + adjective means more than is acceptable or needed; *not* + adjective + *enough* means less than is needed. *Too small* and *not big enough* describe the same problem from opposite sides.
entries.usage: Both are neutral and very common. In neutral statements, *too* signals a problem, so it is not a stronger *very* (*too nice* sounds like a complaint); casual exclamations (*That's too funny!*) and the polite formula *You're too kind* are exceptions. *Not … enough* names the quality that is missing (*not warm enough*).
entries.pattern: too + adjective / adverb; not + adjective / adverb + enough
examples: These jeans are **too tight**. Do you have them in a larger size?
The soup **isn't hot enough**; could you heat it up a little?
Our old car **wasn't big enough** for three car seats.

drill.sentence: This apartment {{isn't big enough}} for a family of five.
drill.hint: Say the same thing with enough: This apartment is too small for a family of five.

mistake.wrong: My new manager is too nice. I really like working for her.
mistake.right: My new manager is really nice. I really like working for her.
mistake.why: *Too* means more than is good, so it sounds like a complaint; for a strong positive, use *really* or *very*.

entries.term: position of enough: enough time / good enough
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Enough* means *as much as needed*; it comes before a noun (*enough time*) but after an adjective or adverb (*good enough*, *fast enough*).
entries.usage: This order is fixed in every register. With an adjective + noun, *enough* usually goes before the whole phrase (*enough clean towels*). A *to*-infinitive or *for* + person follows the whole phrase: *old enough to vote*, *big enough for all of us*.
entries.pattern: enough + noun; adjective / adverb + enough (+ to + verb / for + person)
examples: Do we have **enough chairs** for everyone on Saturday?
Is the water **warm enough** for the kids to swim?
She didn't run **fast enough** to make the final.

drill.sentence: My Spanish isn't {{good enough}} to follow the news yet.
drill.hint: Put enough in the right place: My Spanish isn't enough good to follow the news yet.

mistake.wrong: We don't have money enough for a vacation this year.
mistake.right: We don't have enough money for a vacation this year.
mistake.why: Before a noun, *enough* comes first; *money enough* sounds old-fashioned or literary.

entries.term: either … or: either today or tomorrow
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Either … or* presents two alternatives and says that one of them is true or will happen.
entries.usage: Common in all registers; it makes the choice sharper than *or* alone, sometimes as a warning (*Either you leave now, or you'll miss the bus*). In careful English, *either* goes right before the first of two parallel parts: *either by phone or by email*, *either call or text*.
entries.pattern: either + A + or + B (A and B have the same form)
examples: You can pay **either in cash or by card**.
We'll **either fly or take the train**; we haven't decided yet.
**Either** you apologize to your sister, **or** you're not going to the party.

drill.sentence: You can {{either call or text}} me; I check my phone all day.
drill.hint: Shorten with either … or: You can call me, or you can text me; I check my phone all day.

mistake.wrong: We'll meet either on Friday either on Saturday.
mistake.right: We'll meet either on Friday or on Saturday.
mistake.why: The second choice is introduced by *or*; *either* is not repeated, unlike French *soit … soit* or Spanish *o … o*.

entries.term: not only … but also without inversion: She not only wrote it but also directed it
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Not only … but also* adds a second point, often a more surprising one: *She not only wrote it but also directed it* means she wrote it and, on top of that, directed it.
entries.usage: Common in writing, speeches and fairly formal speech. Inside the sentence, word order stays normal; inversion is needed only when *Not only* starts the sentence (*Not only did she …*). The two parts should match, and *also* can move or be replaced (*but she directed it too*).
entries.pattern: subject + not only + verb / phrase + but also + verb / phrase
examples: The new library is **not only bigger but also** much quieter.
He **not only fixed the leak but also** cleaned up afterward.
The festival attracts **not only locals but also** visitors from all over the state.

drill.sentence: My brother {{not only cooked dinner but also}} washed all the dishes.
drill.hint: Rewrite with not only … but also, keeping normal word order: My brother cooked dinner, and he also washed all the dishes.

mistake.wrong: He not only plays the guitar but also the piano.
mistake.right: He plays not only the guitar but also the piano.
mistake.why: In careful writing, the two parts should match: both are nouns here, so *not only* goes after the verb, right before *the guitar*.

entries.term: present tense after when / as soon as: I'll call you when I get home
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In time clauses about the future (after *when, as soon as, before, after, until*), English uses the present tense; *will* goes only in the main clause.
entries.usage: This rule holds in every register. *Will* after *when* is correct only when the *when*-clause is not a time clause but a question or the object of a verb: *I don't know when he'll arrive*.
entries.pattern: main clause with will / imperative + when / as soon as / before / until + present simple
examples: I'll text you **when I land** so you know I made it.
**As soon as the rain stops**, we'll head out.
Don't open your presents **until everyone gets here**.

drill.sentence: We'll start dinner as soon as your dad {{gets}} home.
drill.hint: Correct the verb (one word): We'll start dinner as soon as your dad will get home.

mistake.wrong: When I will finish college, I'll move to Seattle.
mistake.right: When I finish college, I'll move to Seattle.
mistake.why: In a time clause about the future, use the present tense; *will* goes only in the main clause.

entries.term: who for people, which for things: the man who / the box which
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In relative clauses, *who* refers to people and *which* to things; *that* can refer to both, but only in defining clauses.
entries.usage: Pets with names are often *who* (*our dog, who hates the rain*). For companies and organizations, careful writing uses *that* or *which* (*a company that makes tires*), though *who* is common in speech. Between commas, choose *who* or *which*, since *that* is not possible there.
entries.pattern: person + who (that); thing + which (that)
examples: I have a cousin **who works** as a firefighter in Tucson.
Our new sofa, **which** arrived yesterday, is already covered in cat hair.
It's a show **that** everyone at my office is talking about.

drill.sentence: Our mail carrier, {{who}} has been on this route for years, knows every dog by name.
drill.hint: Choose who or which: Our mail carrier, ___ has been on this route for years, knows every dog by name.

mistake.wrong: This is the book who changed my life.
mistake.right: This is the book that changed my life.
mistake.why: *Who* is only for people (and sometimes pets); for things, use *that* or *which*.

entries.term: subject relative pronoun cannot be dropped: the man who called me
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: When the relative pronoun is the subject of its clause, so that a verb follows it directly, it cannot be left out: *the man who called me*.
entries.usage: This is the other side of *the book I read*: you can drop the pronoun only when a new subject follows it. Without it, the listener hears a complete sentence (*The man called me*) and gets lost. Some casual dialects drop it after *there's* (*There's a guy wants to see you*), but this is nonstandard.
entries.pattern: noun + who / that / which + verb (the pronoun is the subject and must stay)
examples: The woman **who lives upstairs** plays the piano every night.
Anyone **who wants** a ride to the game should be here by six.
I need a phone **that lasts** more than a day on one charge.

drill.sentence: A store {{that}} sells nothing but hot sauce just opened downtown.
drill.hint: Add the missing word (that or who): A store sells nothing but hot sauce just opened downtown.

mistake.wrong: People live near the airport complain about the noise.
mistake.right: People who live near the airport complain about the noise.
mistake.why: The pronoun is the subject of *live*, so it cannot be left out.

entries.term: whose as a possessive relative: the colleague whose laptop broke
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Whose* + noun shows possession inside a relative clause and replaces *his, her, its* or *their*: *the colleague whose laptop broke* means the colleague and his or her broken laptop.
entries.usage: Neutral and common in speech and writing. *Whose* and its noun work as one unit: no article follows *whose* (*whose car*, not *whose the car*), and a preposition can go at the end of the clause (*the friend whose couch I slept on*).
entries.pattern: noun + whose + noun + verb
examples: I sat next to a man **whose dog** had just had puppies.
Is that the family **whose car** is blocking our driveway?
She's the author **whose first novel** was made into a movie.

drill.sentence: That's the neighbor {{whose son}} mows our lawn in the summer.
drill.hint: Join with whose: That's the neighbor. Her son mows our lawn in the summer.

mistake.wrong: That's the man who his wife is a pilot.
mistake.right: That's the man whose wife is a pilot.
mistake.why: *Whose* replaces *who* + *his / her*; do not use *who* followed by a possessive.

entries.term: where vs. which for places: the town where I live / the town I visited
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Use *where* when the place is not the object of the verb in the clause (*the town where I live*); use *that*, *which* or no pronoun when the place is the object (*the town I visited*).
entries.usage: A quick test: if the short version would end with *there* (*I live there*), use *where*; if it would end with *it* (*I visited it*), use *that*, *which* or nothing. This matters with verbs that take a direct object, such as *visit, see, love, recommend* and *choose*.
entries.pattern: place + where + subject + verb (no object) / place + (that / which) + subject + verb that takes an object
examples: The hospital **where I was born** closed down last year.
Kyoto is a city **I'd love to visit** again someday.
That's the restaurant **that my brother recommended**.

drill.sentence: The museum {{that}} we visited in Chicago has an entire floor of dinosaurs.
drill.hint: Choose where or that: The museum ___ we visited in Chicago has an entire floor of dinosaurs.

mistake.wrong: This is the park where we visited on Sunday.
mistake.right: This is the park (that) we visited on Sunday.
mistake.why: *Visit* takes a direct object, so use *that*, *which* or nothing, not *where*.

entries.term: when in relative clauses: the day when we met
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After a time noun (*day, year, moment, time*), *when* introduces a relative clause and means *on which*, *in which* or *at which*.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing. In conversation, *when* is often left out or replaced by *that* (*the day we met*, *the day that we met*). After a date or a year, a clause between commas adds extra information: *in 2020, when everything shut down*.
entries.pattern: time noun + (when / that) + subject + verb
examples: I'll never forget **the day when** we brought our son home.
There are mornings **when** I just can't get out of bed.
My parents met in 1985, **when** they were both working at a summer camp.

drill.sentence: Do you remember the summer {{when}} we drove all the way to Maine?
drill.hint: Choose when or which: Do you remember the summer ___ we drove all the way to Maine?

mistake.wrong: I still remember the day which we met.
mistake.right: I still remember the day (when) we met.
mistake.why: *Which* would need a preposition (*on which*); use *when*, *that* or no pronoun.

entries.term: what as a relative pronoun: I did what you asked
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *What* as a relative pronoun means *the thing(s) that*; it already contains the noun, so nothing comes before it: *I did what you asked*.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing, especially after *do, say, mean, need* and *understand*. Do not put *that*, *the thing* or another noun before *what*; after a noun or *everything*, use *that* or nothing instead.
entries.pattern: verb / preposition + what + subject + verb (= the thing that)
examples: Just tell me **what you need**, and I'll pick it up on my way.
**What he said** at dinner really hurt my feelings.
I'm not sure that's **what the doctor meant**.

drill.sentence: Is this {{what}} you were looking for?
drill.hint: Replace the thing that with one word: Is this the thing that you were looking for?

mistake.wrong: Thanks, that's exactly that what I needed.
mistake.right: Thanks, that's exactly what I needed.
mistake.why: *What* already means *the thing that*, so *that* or *the thing* cannot come before it.

entries.term: despite the fact that + clause: despite the fact that it rained
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Despite the fact that* (or *in spite of the fact that*) lets *despite* introduce a full clause: *despite the fact that it rained* means although it rained.
entries.usage: Formal and a bit wordy; common in reports, news and essays, while speech usually uses *although* or *even though*. *The fact that* cannot be left out: *despite it rained* and *despite that it rained* are both wrong.
entries.pattern: despite / in spite of + the fact that + subject + verb
examples: **Despite the fact that** it was Black Friday, the mall was almost empty.
She took the job **in spite of the fact that** the pay was lower.
**Despite the fact that** the study was small, its results got a lot of attention.

drill.sentence: {{Despite the fact that}} he'd never cooked for twelve people, the dinner was a big success.
drill.hint: Rewrite with despite, keeping the full clause: Although he'd never cooked for twelve people, the dinner was a big success.

mistake.wrong: Despite it was late, they kept working.
mistake.right: Despite the fact that it was late, they kept working.
mistake.why: *Despite* cannot take a clause directly; add *the fact that*, or use *although*.

entries.term: however in the middle: The plan, however, failed
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *However* placed after the subject or the first phrase, between commas, contrasts this sentence with the previous one and puts focus on the words before it.
entries.usage: Common in formal writing and reports, where it sounds smoother than starting every sentence with *However*. It often contrasts two people or things (*Most guests left; Sam, however, stayed*). Use a comma on both sides.
entries.pattern: Subject, however, verb … / first phrase, however, rest of the sentence
examples: Most guests left by midnight. My cousin, **however**, stayed until two.
The restaurant isn't cheap; the portions, **however**, are huge.
The plan looked great on paper. In practice, **however**, it caused endless delays.

drill.sentence: The first week of our trip was rainy. {{The second week, however,}} was perfect.
drill.hint: Move however after the subject: The first week of our trip was rainy. However, the second week was perfect.

mistake.wrong: Most of my friends loved the movie. I however found it boring.
mistake.right: Most of my friends loved the movie. I, however, found it boring.
mistake.why: In the middle of a sentence, *however* needs a comma on both sides.

entries.term: nevertheless / nonetheless: The risk is high; nevertheless, we'll try
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Nevertheless* and *nonetheless* mean *in spite of that* or *but still*: the second statement is true although the first one would make you expect the opposite.
entries.usage: Formal; common in writing, speeches and careful speech, while conversation uses *still*, *even so* or *anyway*. They usually start a sentence or follow a semicolon, with a comma after them, or come at the end of a clause (*…, but we went ahead nonetheless*). Unlike *however*, which only shows contrast, they stress that the second fact holds despite the first.
entries.pattern: Sentence; nevertheless / nonetheless, sentence / …, but … nonetheless
examples: The forecast looked bad. **Nevertheless**, thousands of people showed up for the parade.
It's a tiny apartment with no view, but I love it **nonetheless**.
The surgery carries some risk; **nevertheless**, most patients in her situation choose to have it.

drill.sentence: The roads were icy; {{nevertheless, the buses}} kept to their schedule.
drill.hint: Rewrite with nevertheless after the semicolon (drop but and anyway): The roads were icy, but the buses kept to their schedule anyway.

mistake.wrong: My brother loves hiking. Nevertheless, my sister prefers the beach.
mistake.right: My brother loves hiking. My sister, however, prefers the beach.
mistake.why: Nothing here is surprising, only a contrast between two people, so *nevertheless* doesn't fit; use *however* or *but*.

entries.term: while meaning although: While I agree, I have some doubts
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *While* at the start of a sentence can mean *although*: it admits one point before making a contrasting one.
entries.usage: Common in discussions, emails and essays, where it sounds balanced and polite (*While I understand your concern, …*). It usually comes first, because after the main clause *while* is easily read as *at the same time*. Like *although*, it takes a full clause.
entries.pattern: While + clause (the point you accept), main clause (the contrast)
examples: **While** I see your point, I still think we should wait.
**While** the food was a bit overpriced, the view from our table was amazing.
**While** the new bike lanes are popular, some shop owners worry about losing parking.

drill.sentence: {{While I appreciate the offer}}, I'm going to have to say no.
drill.hint: Rewrite with while, starting with the point you accept: I appreciate the offer, but I'm going to have to say no.

mistake.wrong: Whereas I understand your concern, I can't change the rules.
mistake.right: While I understand your concern, I can't change the rules.
mistake.why: *Whereas* compares two different facts (*She likes tea, whereas I prefer coffee*); to admit a point before a contrast, use *while* or *although*.

entries.term: yet as a conjunction: simple yet effective
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Yet* can mean *but* and links two ideas when the second is surprising after the first: *simple yet effective*.
entries.usage: Common in writing, reviews and ads, especially between two adjectives (*elegant yet comfortable*). Between clauses, it is more formal than *but* and stresses the surprise (*He's rich, yet he lives very simply*); in speech, *and yet* is common.
entries.pattern: adjective + yet + adjective / clause, (and) yet + clause
examples: It's a **simple yet delicious** soup that takes twenty minutes to make.
He trains every single day, **yet** he still can't beat his younger sister.
It sounds crazy, **and yet** it actually works.

drill.sentence: The instructions were short {{yet}} surprisingly clear.
drill.hint: Replace but with a more formal word that stresses the surprise: The instructions were short but surprisingly clear.

mistake.wrong: The room was small but yet very comfortable.
mistake.right: The room was small yet very comfortable.
mistake.why: In writing, *but yet* is redundant because *yet* already means *but*; *and yet* is the normal pair.

entries.term: so as not to / in order not to: so as not to wake her
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *So as not to* and *in order not to* + verb express a negative purpose: you do something to avoid a result (*so as not to wake her* = so that she wouldn't wake up).
entries.usage: Both are fairly formal; in conversation, Americans more often say *so I wouldn't …* (*I whispered so I wouldn't wake her*). *Not* comes before *to*, and a bare *not to* rarely expresses purpose (*I left early not to miss the bus* sounds odd).
entries.pattern: so as not to / in order not to + base verb
examples: I took my shoes off at the door **so as not to wake** the baby.
We spoke in whispers **so as not to disturb** the other people in the waiting room.
The company delayed the announcement **in order not to upset** customers before the holidays.

drill.sentence: I wrote the date on my hand {{so as not to forget}} it.
drill.hint: Rewrite with so as + infinitive: I wrote the date on my hand so that I wouldn't forget it.

mistake.wrong: I turned off my phone for not being disturbed.
mistake.right: I turned off my phone so as not to be disturbed.
mistake.why: Negative purpose is *so as not to* or *in order not to* + base verb (or *so that I wouldn't*), not *for not* + *-ing*.

entries.term: for + noun for purpose: We went out for dinner
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *For* + noun says what someone goes somewhere or does something to get or take part in: *We went out for dinner*, *I'm here for the interview*.
entries.usage: Very common with *go, come, stop* and *ask* (*go out for a drink*, *stop for gas*, *ask for help*). With a verb, use *to*, not *for*: *for dinner* but *to eat*. *For* + *-ing* describes what a thing is used for (*a brush for cleaning bottles*), not why a person did something.
entries.pattern: verb + for + noun (purpose) / verb + to + base verb
examples: Let's stop **for coffee** before we get on the highway.
She moved to Boston **for grad school** and never left.
Can we go out **for pizza** tonight? I don't feel like cooking.

drill.sentence: We're flying to Montana next week {{for}} a friend's wedding.
drill.hint: Choose to or for: We're flying to Montana next week ___ a friend's wedding.

mistake.wrong: I called the bank for asking about my card.
mistake.right: I called the bank to ask about my card.
mistake.why: To say why a person did something, use *to* + verb or *for* + noun; *for* + *-ing* describes what a thing is used for.

entries.term: since / as for reasons: Since you're here, you can help
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Since* and *as* can mean *because*, usually for a reason the listener already knows or will easily accept.
entries.usage: *Since* is very common in American speech and writing (*Since you're here, …*); *as* in this sense sounds more formal and is less common in American speech. Both often start the sentence, before the main point. When the reason is new or is the main point, especially in answer to *why*, use *because*.
entries.pattern: Since / As + clause (known reason), main clause
examples: **Since** you're up, could you grab me a glass of water?
**Since** the store was closed, we ordered pizza instead.
**As** this is your first visit, please fill out the new patient form.

drill.sentence: {{Since it's your birthday}}, I'll do the dishes tonight.
drill.hint: Start with since: I'll do the dishes tonight because it's your birthday.

mistake.wrong: "Why are you late?" "Since the bus broke down."
mistake.right: "Why are you late?" "Because the bus broke down."
mistake.why: To answer a *why* question with a new reason, use *because*, not *since* or *as*.

entries.term: so … that / such … that for results: It was so cold that we stayed in
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *So* + adjective or adverb + *that* and *such* + noun phrase + *that* say that a quality was so strong that it caused a result.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing; in conversation, *that* is often dropped (*I was so tired I fell asleep on the couch*). The choice between *so* and *such* follows the same rule as without *that*: *so* + adjective, *such (a)* + noun phrase.
entries.pattern: so + adjective / adverb + (that) + clause; such (a) + adjective + noun + (that) + clause
examples: The music was **so loud that** we couldn't hear each other.
It was **such a nice day that** we had lunch in the park.
She talks **so fast** I can barely keep up with her.

drill.sentence: The line was {{so long that}} we gave up and went home.
drill.hint: Join with so … that: The line was very long. We gave up and went home.

mistake.wrong: It was so cold day that we stayed inside.
mistake.right: It was such a cold day that we stayed inside.
mistake.why: Before a noun phrase, use *such (a)*; *so* goes with an adjective alone (*It was so cold that …*).

entries.term: so much / so many + noun: so many people
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Before a noun, *so much* (uncountable) and *so many* (plural) express a surprisingly large amount: *so many people*, *so much traffic*.
entries.usage: Very common in speech for surprise or complaint. *Such* cannot go directly before *many* or *much* (*such many* is wrong), although *such a lot of* is possible. Choose *much* or *many* by the noun, as with *how much* and *how many*.
entries.pattern: so many + plural noun; so much + uncountable noun
examples: Why are there **so many people** in line at the post office today?
I have **so much paperwork** to finish before my vacation that I'm working Saturday.
Why do you need **so many pairs of shoes**?

drill.sentence: Sorry I'm late. There was {{so much}} traffic on the bridge.
drill.hint: Rewrite with so + much or many: Sorry I'm late. There was a lot of traffic on the bridge.

mistake.wrong: There were such many people at the concert.
mistake.right: There were so many people at the concert.
mistake.why: *Such* cannot go before *many* or *much*; use *so many* or *so much*.

entries.term: too … to: too tired to drive
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Too* + adjective or adverb + *to* + verb says that the degree is so high that the action is impossible: *too tired to drive* means so tired that I can't drive.
entries.usage: Very common and neutral. Add *for* + person when someone else would do the action (*too hot for the kids to play outside*). Do not add an object pronoun that refers back to the subject: *The box is too heavy to lift*, not *to lift it*.
entries.pattern: too + adjective / adverb (+ for + person) + to + base verb
examples: Grandpa's **too proud to ask** for help, even when he needs it.
It's **too cold for the kids to play** outside today.
The print on the label was **too small to read** without my glasses.

drill.sentence: He was {{too nervous to eat}} anything before the interview.
drill.hint: Rewrite with too … to: He was so nervous that he couldn't eat anything before the interview.

mistake.wrong: This tea is too hot to drink it.
mistake.right: This tea is too hot to drink.
mistake.why: The subject (*this tea*) is already what you drink, so do not add *it*.

entries.term: both … and: both fast and cheap
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Both … and* stresses that two things are true together: *both fast and cheap* means fast and also cheap.
entries.usage: Common in all registers and stronger than plain *and*. Put *both* right before the first of two parallel parts (*both in Chicago and in Denver*, or *in both Chicago and Denver*). Two subjects joined by *both … and* take a plural verb.
entries.pattern: both + A + and + B (A and B have the same form)
examples: This blender is **both quieter and cheaper** than the one we had before.
**Both my parents and my in-laws** are coming for Christmas.
She's **both a nurse and a published poet**.

drill.sentence: The trip was {{both relaxing and educational}}.
drill.hint: Rewrite with both … and: The trip was relaxing, and it was educational too.

mistake.wrong: Both my brother and my sister is coming to the wedding.
mistake.right: Both my brother and my sister are coming to the wedding.
mistake.why: Two subjects joined by *both … and* take a plural verb.

entries.term: neither … nor: neither fast nor cheap
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Neither … nor* says that two things are both not true: *neither fast nor cheap* means not fast and not cheap.
entries.usage: It sounds a little formal or emphatic; in conversation, people often say *not … or* (*It's not fast or cheap*). The verb stays positive, because *neither* already makes the sentence negative. After a negative verb, use *either … or* instead (*I don't eat either meat or fish*).
entries.pattern: neither + A + nor + B (with a positive verb)
examples: The movie was **neither funny nor scary**, just long.
**Neither my husband nor I** heard the smoke alarm.
She **neither called nor texted**, so I assumed she wasn't coming.

drill.sentence: The apartment {{was neither cheap nor close to downtown}}.
drill.hint: Rewrite with neither … nor: The apartment wasn't cheap, and it wasn't close to downtown either.

mistake.wrong: She doesn't eat neither meat nor fish.
mistake.right: She eats neither meat nor fish.
mistake.why: *Neither … nor* is already negative, so the verb stays positive (or say *She doesn't eat meat or fish*).

entries.term: as soon as + present perfect: as soon as I've finished
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In a future time clause, *as soon as* + present perfect stresses that the first action will be finished before the second one starts: *as soon as I've finished* means right after I finish.
entries.usage: Common in emails and conversation. The present simple often means the same (*as soon as I finish*); the present perfect makes the completion clearer. Never use *will* or *will have* in the time clause.
entries.pattern: will / imperative … + as soon as + have / has + past participle
examples: I'll send you the photos **as soon as I've edited** them.
**As soon as you've paid**, you'll get a confirmation email.
Text me **as soon as the doctor has seen** you.

drill.sentence: We'll leave for the airport {{as soon as I've packed}}.
drill.hint: Rewrite with as soon as + present perfect: First I'll pack, and then we'll leave for the airport.

mistake.wrong: I'll call you as soon as I will have finished.
mistake.right: I'll call you as soon as I've finished.
mistake.why: A future time clause uses the present perfect, not the future perfect.

entries.term: by the time + present for the future: By the time you arrive, I'll have left
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *By the time* + present tense names a future moment, and the main clause, often in the future perfect, says what will already have happened before it.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, often with a slightly negative tone (*By the time we get there, all the food will be gone*). The *by the time* clause uses the present, never *will*. *Will have* + past participle stresses that something is complete before that moment.
entries.pattern: By the time + present simple, will have + past participle
examples: **By the time you get** this message, **I'll have left** for the airport.
**By the time the kids wake up**, **I'll have finished** my run.
**By the time** the bridge **is finished**, it **will have cost** twice the original estimate.

drill.sentence: By the time we get to the theater, the movie {{will have started}}.
drill.hint: Complete with start in the right form: By the time we get to the theater, the movie ___.

mistake.wrong: Hurry! By the time we get there, the store will close.
mistake.right: Hurry! By the time we get there, the store will have closed.
mistake.why: *Will close* only says when it closes; *will have closed* says it will already be closed when we arrive.

entries.term: once meaning as soon as: Once you've signed, we can start
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Once* + clause means *as soon as* or *after*: when the first thing has happened, the second follows or becomes possible.
entries.usage: Very common in instructions, plans and emails (*Once you've logged in, …*). Like other time clauses, it takes the present or present perfect for the future. It often suggests that the first step is a condition: *Once you get used to it, it's easy*.
entries.pattern: Once + present / present perfect, main clause
examples: **Once you get used to** the cold, Minnesota winters aren't that bad.
**Once the paint has dried**, you can put on the second coat.
We'll ship your order **once your payment clears**.

drill.sentence: {{Once you've signed}} the lease, we'll give you the keys.
drill.hint: Rewrite with once + present perfect: You'll sign the lease, and right after that we'll give you the keys.

mistake.wrong: Once that you've signed the form, we can begin.
mistake.right: Once you've signed the form, we can begin.
mistake.why: *Once* is a complete conjunction; do not add *that* after it.

entries.term: before / after + -ing: Before leaving, check the lights
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: When both clauses have the same subject, *before* and *after* can be followed by an *-ing* form instead of a full clause: *Before leaving, check the lights*.
entries.usage: Common in instructions, writing and fairly careful speech; in conversation, a full clause is just as natural (*before you leave*). Use *-ing*, not *to* + verb, after these prepositions. The *-ing* form refers to the subject of the main clause, so make sure the two match.
entries.pattern: before / after + -ing (same subject), main clause
examples: **Before leaving**, please make sure all the windows are closed.
**After graduating** from college, she spent a year teaching English in Japan.
Always wash your hands **before handling** food.

drill.sentence: {{After eating}} lunch, we took a long walk along the river.
drill.hint: Rewrite with after + -ing: After we ate lunch, we took a long walk along the river.

mistake.wrong: Before to go to bed, I always read for a while.
mistake.right: Before going to bed, I always read for a while.
mistake.why: *Before* and *after* are prepositions here, so they take *-ing*, not *to* + verb.

entries.term: apart from: Apart from John, everyone came
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Apart from* has two meanings: *except for* (*Apart from John, everyone came*) and *in addition to* (*Apart from being cheap, it's also fast*).
entries.usage: Neutral; *aside from* means the same and is especially common in American English. With *everyone, nothing* or *all*, it usually means *except*; with *also* or *too*, it means *in addition to*. It is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form.
entries.pattern: apart from / aside from + noun / -ing
examples: **Apart from** a little rain on Tuesday, the weather was perfect.
**Apart from** being a great cook, he's also a talented painter.
I don't know anyone in Phoenix **apart from** my cousin.

drill.sentence: {{Apart from being cheaper}}, the new gym is also much closer to home.
drill.hint: Rewrite with apart from: The new gym is cheaper, and it's also much closer to home.

mistake.wrong: Apart of my brother, everyone came to the party.
mistake.right: Apart from my brother, everyone came to the party.
mistake.why: The fixed phrase is *apart from*; *a part of* means a piece of something.

entries.term: no but after although: Although it was late, we stayed
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Although* already links the two clauses and shows the contrast, so the main clause does not start with *but*.
entries.usage: Use one linker per contrast: either *Although A, B* or *A, but B*. Doubling them is a common transfer error for speakers of languages that pair the two words, such as Chinese and Russian. *Still* can appear in the main clause (*Although it was late, we still stayed*).
entries.pattern: Although + clause, main clause (no but) / clause, but + clause
examples: **Although** the store was crowded, we found everything we needed.
**Although** he apologized, she's still upset with him.
The car is twenty years old, **but** it's never let us down.

drill.sentence: {{Although we were exhausted}}, we stayed until the very end.
drill.hint: Rewrite with although, without but: We were exhausted, but we stayed until the very end.

mistake.wrong: Although the rent is high, but the location is great.
mistake.right: Although the rent is high, the location is great.
mistake.why: *Although* already introduces the contrast, so the main clause takes no *but*.

entries.term: rather than + verb: Let's walk rather than drive
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Rather than* + verb says that one action is chosen instead of another: *Let's walk rather than drive*.
entries.usage: Neutral and common in speech and writing. After a base form or *to*-infinitive, the second verb is usually a base form too (*walk rather than drive*); at the start of a sentence, *-ing* is more common (*Rather than waiting, we left*). *Instead of* always takes *-ing* and sounds a little more casual.
entries.pattern: base verb + rather than + base verb / Rather than + -ing, main clause
examples: Why don't we cook at home tonight **rather than order** takeout?
**Rather than waiting** for the bus, we decided to walk.
The city plans to repair the old bridge **rather than build** a new one.

drill.sentence: It's such a nice evening. Let's walk {{rather than}} take a cab.
drill.hint: Rewrite so that take stays in its base form: It's such a nice evening. Let's walk instead of taking a cab.

mistake.wrong: Rather than to complain, why don't you help?
mistake.right: Rather than complaining, why don't you help?
mistake.why: At the start of a sentence, *rather than* takes *-ing* (or a base form), not *to* + verb.

entries.term: so that vs. so: I left early so that I could rest / It rained, so we stayed
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *So that* introduces a purpose (why someone did something); *so* after a comma introduces a result (what happened because of it).
entries.usage: In speech, *so* alone can also express purpose (*I left early so I could rest*), but then there is no comma and usually a modal (*can, could, would*). A comma + *so* signals a result: *It rained, so we stayed home*. If the clause answers *why*, use *so that*; if it answers *what happened next*, use a comma and *so*.
entries.pattern: clause + so that + subject + modal (purpose) / clause, so + clause (result)
examples: I turned my phone off **so that** I could focus on my book.
The bus never came, **so** we took a taxi.
I'll leave a key under the mat **so that** you can let yourself in.

drill.sentence: My phone died, {{so}} I couldn't call you.
drill.hint: Choose so or so that: My phone died, ___ I couldn't call you.

mistake.wrong: Our flight was canceled so that we stayed another night.
mistake.right: Our flight was canceled, so we stayed another night.
mistake.why: This is a result, not a purpose; *so that* would mean the flight was canceled in order to make you stay.

entries.term: adjective + that-clause: I'm sure it'll work
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Adjectives of feeling or certainty (*sure, glad, afraid, sorry, happy, worried*) can be followed by a *that*-clause, and *that* is often left out: *I'm glad (that) you came*.
entries.usage: Dropping *that* is the normal choice in conversation and casual emails; keeping it sounds more careful. *I'm afraid* + clause is a polite way to give bad news, not an expression of fear (*I'm afraid we're fully booked*). No preposition comes before the clause: *sure of the answer*, but *sure (that) she's right*.
entries.pattern: be + sure / glad / afraid / sorry / happy / worried + (that) + clause
examples: **I'm sure** you'll love the new place once you've unpacked.
**I'm afraid** we're out of the salmon tonight, but the trout is excellent.
We're **so glad** you could make it all the way from Texas!

drill.sentence: {{I'm afraid}} we don't have any tables left for tonight.
drill.hint: Give the bad news politely with an adjective (not sorry): Unfortunately, we don't have any tables left for tonight.

mistake.wrong: I'm sure of that she'll get the job.
mistake.right: I'm sure (that) she'll get the job.
mistake.why: Before a clause, the adjective takes *that* or nothing, not a preposition: *sure of* + noun, but *sure (that)* + clause.

entries.term: after that / afterward: After that, we had dinner
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *After that* and *afterward* mean *later* or *next*, pointing back to an event just mentioned; *after* alone normally needs a noun or a clause.
entries.usage: *Afterward* is the more common American form, especially in writing; *afterwards* is usual in British English and also heard in the US. *After that* often starts a sentence in a sequence, while *afterward* often comes at the end (*We had dinner afterward*). In casual speech, *after* alone at the end is also common (*Let's grab food after*), but avoid it in formal writing.
entries.pattern: After that, + clause / clause + afterward / after + noun or clause
examples: We hiked to the lake in the morning. **After that**, we had a picnic.
The concert ended at eleven, and we went out for pizza **afterward**.
He had knee surgery in May and was on crutches for weeks **afterward**.

drill.sentence: First we checked in at the hotel. {{After that}}, we went to find something to eat.
drill.hint: Correct the linker by adding one word: First we checked in at the hotel. After, we went to find something to eat.

mistake.wrong: Afterward I finish this report, I'll call you.
mistake.right: After I finish this report, I'll call you.
mistake.why: *Afterward* is an adverb; to introduce a clause, use the conjunction *after*.

entries.term: everything that, not everything what: Everything she said was true
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After *everything, all, nothing, anything* and *something*, a relative clause uses *that* or no pronoun: *Everything (that) she said was true*. *What* is not possible here.
entries.usage: A very common error for speakers of German (*alles, was*), French (*tout ce que*) and other languages with a *what*-word here. In speech, the pronoun is usually dropped when a subject follows (*Is there anything I can do?*). When the pronoun is the subject, keep *that*: *all that matters*.
entries.pattern: everything / all / nothing / anything + (that) + subject + verb
examples: Thanks for **everything you did** for us this week.
There's **nothing I can do** about it now, unfortunately.
**All that matters** is that nobody got hurt.

drill.sentence: I've packed everything {{that}} we need for the camping trip.
drill.hint: Correct the pronoun: I've packed everything what we need for the camping trip.

mistake.wrong: Nothing what he does surprises me anymore.
mistake.right: Nothing he does surprises me anymore.
mistake.why: After *nothing, everything* and *all*, use *that* or no pronoun; *what* already means *the thing that*.
